title: ASEAN, Still Toothless, Is Losing Its Faith in the U.S. | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: At the late-July 2026 ASEAN Foreign Ministers' Meeting in Manila, Washington undercut Rubio's reassurance tour by imposing fresh tariffs on the Philippines and six other ASEAN members while the renewed Iran war spiked energy prices in the region most dependent on Persian Gulf oil and LNG. Kurlantzick argues the hedging era is ending — Pew and ISEAS polling now show China favored over the United States across Southeast Asia, treaty ally Thailand is tilting to Beijing, and ASEAN itself remains structurally unable to act because China's client states can veto consensus.

themes.theme: U.S. credibility collapse in Southeast Asia

insights.claim: The Trump administration imposed new tariffs on the Philippines — a treaty ally and the strongest U.S. supporter in the region — plus six other ASEAN members during the very week Rubio was in Manila promising Indo-Pacific commitment.
insights.speaker: Joshua Kurlantzick
insights.so_what: Tariffing a treaty ally mid-summit tells regional capitals that security alignment buys no trade protection — a durable repricing of the value of a U.S. alliance.
insights.quote: While the summit was taking place, the Trump administration imposed new tariffs on the Philippines—a treaty ally and the strongest U.S. supporter in the region—as well as six other ASEAN members.

insights.claim: Negotiating tariff deals with Washington has lost its rationale for Southeast Asian governments because U.S. tariffs are subject to revision whenever Washington finds a fresh rationale, with the latest levies nominally justified by forced-labor and reciprocity findings that seemed almost arbitrary.
insights.speaker: Joshua Kurlantzick
insights.so_what: If counterparties conclude deals are not durable, expect fewer concessions and slower negotiations in the next tariff round — supply-chain relocation decisions get made around, not with, Washington.
insights.quote: The new levies provided regional leaders with further evidence that negotiating with the United States over tariffs, as many ASEAN members had done the year before, makes no sense.
insights.locator: The new levies provided regional leaders

insights.claim: Rubio's most tangible deliverable to the region was roughly $100 million in military financing for the Philippines plus money to expand a coast guard pier on Palawan near contested South China Sea waters — a sum officials privately compared unfavorably with Chinese aid and investment.
insights.speaker: Joshua Kurlantzick
insights.so_what: A $100 million package against Chinese infrastructure-scale finance quantifies the gap; U.S. influence in the region is now a rounding error in capital terms.

insights.claim: Rubio's reassurance may not even represent the White House: ASEAN officials concluded his words had little meaning and that he was possibly out of sync with the administration he speaks for.
insights.speaker: Joshua Kurlantzick
insights.so_what: When counterparties discount the secretary of state's assurances, diplomatic signaling stops moving regional risk premia — only concrete actions like tariffs and troop deployments will.
insights.quote: “I believe very much that the future and the story of the twenty-first century will be written in this region,” Rubio said.
insights.locator: In late July, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio

themes.theme: Iran war as a Southeast Asian energy shock

insights.claim: Southeast Asia is perhaps the region most dependent on oil and liquefied natural gas from the Persian Gulf, and has already absorbed one massive energy shock during the first phase of the Iran war.
insights.speaker: Joshua Kurlantzick
insights.so_what: ASEAN economies are the highest-beta losers from a Hormuz closure — watch regional currencies, fertilizer costs, and current accounts before Western energy names.
insights.quote: Southeast Asia is perhaps the region most dependent on oil and liquefied natural gas from the Persian Gulf, and has already faced one massive energy shock during the first part of the war.
insights.locator: Anger toward Washington spilled out at the meeting

insights.claim: ASEAN foreign ministers issued both a joint statement seeking assurances the Strait of Hormuz would stay open and a more explicit joint communiqué warning that renewed war would decimate the region's energy access, worsen poverty, impede trade, and harm food production through disrupted fertilizer supply.
insights.speaker: Joshua Kurlantzick
insights.so_what: The energy-to-fertilizer-to-food chain is the second-order transmission channel; a Hormuz event would show up in Asian food inflation within a quarter.
insights.locator: ASEAN foreign ministers released a joint statement

insights.claim: Renewed U.S.–Iran fighting during the ASEAN summit week, with Trump considering and then deferring a ground invasion, sent energy prices skyrocketing.
insights.speaker: Joshua Kurlantzick
insights.so_what: The invasion decision remains live and unpriced — a deferred ground invasion is optionality on another energy spike, not its removal.
insights.quote: Those choices sent energy prices skyrocketing, which is a big problem for Southeast Asia.
insights.locator: The same week of the ASEAN summit

themes.theme: China overtakes the U.S. in global favorability

insights.claim: A mid-July Pew Research Center survey of more than forty-two thousand people across thirty-six countries found China now viewed more favorably than the United States in most of them, reversing a pattern that had held for nearly two decades.
insights.speaker: Joshua Kurlantzick
insights.so_what: A two-decade soft-power reversal is a structural input to market access, procurement decisions, and standards adoption over years, not news-cycle noise.
insights.quote: showing that China is now seen more favorably than the United States in most of them—a reversal of a pattern that had held for nearly two decades
insights.locator: In mid-July, the Pew Research Center published a survey

insights.claim: The favorability gaps in Southeast Asia are enormous, not marginal: Pew found respondents favor China over the United States by thirty-nine points in Singapore, thirty-three in Thailand, forty-three in Indonesia, and fifty-six in Malaysia.
insights.speaker: Joshua Kurlantzick
insights.so_what: Singapore — long one of the closest U.S. partners in the region — printing a 39-point deficit means even the most reliable hedgers face domestic political cost for siding with Washington.
insights.quote: The Pew study found that in Singapore, long one of the closest U.S. partners in the region, respondents now favor China over the United States by a whopping thirty-nine points.
insights.locator: The Pew poll showed that countries across Asia

insights.claim: The Pew result is corroborated by two independent datasets: Gallup's 2025 global ratings show China's median approval at 36 percent versus 31 percent for the United States across more than 130 countries, and an ISEAS–Yusof Ishak Institute regional poll had ASEAN respondents forced to choose picking China over the United States 52 to 48.
insights.speaker: Joshua Kurlantzick
insights.so_what: Three separate instruments converging removes the methodology objection — this is a real level shift, and Gallup calls it the widest China-favorable margin in nearly twenty years.
insights.quote: In Gallup’s global ratings for 2025, China’s median approval rating (36 percent) edged past that of the United States (31 percent) across more than 130 countries—the widest margin in China’s favor that Gallup has recorded in nearly twenty years.
insights.locator: The poll hardly came out of the blue

insights.claim: ASEAN's consensus rule is a de facto Chinese veto: Beijing has several de facto client states inside the bloc, such as Cambodia and Laos, and through them can block consensus on anything it dislikes.
insights.speaker: Joshua Kurlantzick
insights.so_what: Treat ASEAN as structurally incapable of collective action against Chinese interests — regional risk must be hedged bilaterally, never through the bloc.
insights.quote: The reason for the lack of unity is obvious: China has several de facto client states in ASEAN, such as Cambodia and Laos, and through them can block consensus on anything it dislikes.

insights.claim: Chinese and Philippine forces had several clashes in disputed South China Sea waters during the foreign ministers' meeting itself, and ASEAN still could not produce any consensus statement on the incidents or advance the long-discussed code of conduct.
insights.speaker: Joshua Kurlantzick
insights.so_what: Live maritime clashes failing to produce even a statement sets the escalation floor low — Beijing faces no regional cost for further incidents.
insights.locator: Even the fact that Chinese and Philippine forces

insights.claim: ASEAN has effectively accepted Myanmar's junta-turned-civilian government, meeting Myanmar's leaders in July for the first time in five years and staying largely silent on the stage-managed winter election that installed former junta head Min Aung Hlaing.
insights.speaker: Joshua Kurlantzick
insights.so_what: Regional normalization of the junta lowers the odds of sanctions coordination and raises the odds Myanmar's conflict spillovers — refugees, drugs, disease — become a permanent regional cost.
insights.quote: At this point, ASEAN seems to have simply accepted the Naypyidaw regime.
insights.locator: The meeting failed to yield any commitments

insights.claim: Myanmar's junta is winning militarily on the back of increased assistance from a bloc of autocratic states including Belarus, China, and Russia, even as the country becomes a de facto failed state and the deadliest conflict in Asia.
insights.speaker: Joshua Kurlantzick
insights.so_what: An autocratic-supply coalition sustaining a winning junta is a template for other conflicts; it also entrenches China's access to Myanmar's corridor to the Indian Ocean.
insights.locator: With ASEAN mostly silent, the election

insights.claim: Escalating U.S. unreliability is pushing some Southeast Asian states to abandon hedging between Washington and Beijing altogether, with even U.S. treaty ally Thailand now clearly leaning toward China.
insights.speaker: Joshua Kurlantzick
insights.so_what: A treaty ally openly tilting is the strongest available signal that the U.S. security guarantee no longer anchors the region; expect follow-on defense-procurement and currency-settlement shifts toward Beijing.
insights.quote: But Washington, showing ever-increasing unreliability, is making some Southeast Asian states abandon hedging altogether—even U.S. treaty ally Thailand is now clearly leaning toward China.
insights.locator: For years, Southeast Asian governments have tried to hedge

insights.claim: Even states that still want to hedge, such as Singapore, are finding it harder as public sentiment turns against the United States and Chinese soft power becomes more impressive — meaning the constraint is now domestic politics, not elite preference.
insights.speaker: Joshua Kurlantzick
insights.so_what: Once public opinion binds elite choices, the shift becomes hard to reverse with diplomacy alone — a future U.S. administration cannot simply reset it.
insights.locator: Other states that still want to hedge
